parts.title: Arranging pet care
parts.context: A woman arranges for her dog and parrot to be looked after.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a pet-sitting service to arrange care for her pets. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: Pawsitive Pet Care, Hazel speaking.

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Hello. I'm going away on holiday, and I need someone to look after my pets. I have two of them, and they're quite different.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: That's fine. I'll take some details, and then we can talk about what they need.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller has two pets, so 'two' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Emma Brooks. That's B-R-O-O-K-S.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: Thank you, Mrs Brooks. What are your pets?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: A dog called Biscuit, and a parrot called Mango.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: How old is Biscuit?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: He's eight, so he's not so lively as he was, but he still loves his walks.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: And when will you be away?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: From the ninth of July.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: How long for?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Ten days. We'll be back on the nineteenth.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: How often does Biscuit need walking?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening, for about half an hour each time.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: Has he got any special needs?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: He mustn't be given bones. He has sensitive teeth, and the vet advised us to avoid them. He eats dry food, and the right amount is written on the bag.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: And the parrot?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Mango has to be covered at nine in the evening, or she doesn't sleep. She talks all day, so don't be surprised if she sounds like me.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: That's lovely. How will I get into the house?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: I'll leave a key with my neighbour, Mrs Patel, at number twelve. She'll give it to you. Please ring her before you come.

script.speaker: hazel
script.text: And in case of an emergency?

script.speaker: emma
script.text: Our vet is Dr Singh, that's S-I-N-G-H, and her number is on the fridge, together with mine. Thank you so much, Hazel.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Volunteering at an animal shelter
parts.context: A manager briefs new volunteers at an animal shelter.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of an animal shelter talking to new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: Welcome, everybody, and thank you for offering to help at Greenfield Animal Shelter. I'm Mike Ross, the manager, and I'll explain how we work.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: At the moment, we look after about a hundred and twenty animals. Most are dogs and cats, but we also have rabbits, some birds, and, at the moment, a very friendly goat.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: People often think that most of our animals are given up by owners who can't keep them. In fact, most are strays, brought in by members of the public who find them wandering in the streets.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: On average, an animal stays with us for about six weeks, although some are rehomed in days, and a few of the older ones stay for months.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: Before an animal can be rehomed, it has a full check by the vet, and receives all its vaccinations. We also check the new home before the animal moves.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: We receive no government money. Almost everything we spend comes from donations, so every pound counts, and our charity shop on the high street helps a great deal.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: Now, what will you be doing? Volunteers walk the dogs, which they love, and they clean the kennels and the cat pens, which they love rather less. Medicine is only given by the vet nurses, and training is done by our staff, so you won't need to worry about those.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: You must be at least eighteen years old to volunteer, because you'll be working with animals that are sometimes frightened or unpredictable.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: Everyone starts with an induction, which takes one morning. We show you round, explain the safety rules, and you'll meet the animals you'll be looking after.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: A last word about safety. If you are bitten or scratched, however slightly, please tell me or a member of staff at once. It's very rare, but we must record every incident and clean the wound properly.

script.speaker: ross
script.text: Now, if you're ready, we'll start the tour with the dogs, which is usually everyone's favourite.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Music composition assignments
parts.context: Two music students discuss their compositions and concert.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two music students, Noor and Felix, discussing their composition assignments. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: Noor, how's the composition going? Dr Marsh said that the final piece must be for a small group of players.

script.speaker: noor
script.text: I've settled on a piece for piano and flute. I thought about adding a violin, but I couldn't find a player.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: Why the flute?

script.speaker: noor
script.text: It can sound like the wind, which suits my theme, a journey across the sea. How long is yours supposed to be?

script.speaker: felix
script.text: The brief says between four and six minutes. Mine is exactly five.

script.speaker: noor
script.text: Have you written it all out yet?

script.speaker: felix
script.text: I'm using notation software, because my handwriting is terrible, but I always start at the piano, trying out ideas.

script.speaker: noor
script.text: My problem is the ending. Mine just seems to stop.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: Dr Marsh said that endings are the hardest part. The best advice she gave me was to repeat the opening idea, but more slowly, so that it feels like coming home.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: Who's going to perform the pieces? We need players for the concert.

script.speaker: noor
script.text: The department can find students from the performance course, but we have to book rehearsals by Friday, or all the slots will be taken.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: I'm going to play my own piece on the guitar, so I don't need to find anyone.

script.speaker: noor
script.text: Lucky you. The concert is in the chapel, so the acoustics are very good, although it's cold in there, so wear a coat.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: How will we be marked?

script.speaker: noor
script.text: Half for the composition itself, and half for a written commentary, explaining the choices we made.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: When is the commentary due?

script.speaker: noor
script.text: A week after the concert, so you can include comments from the audience.

script.speaker: felix
script.text: Right, I'll write notes in the rehearsal breaks. Let's meet next week to compare.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how earthquakes are measured
parts.context: A geology lecture on earthquake waves and scales.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how earthquakes are measured. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural events, and yet, until the twentieth century, there was no reliable way to compare one with another. Today I'll explain how scientists measure them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: First, what causes an earthquake? The Earth's crust is divided into huge pieces called tectonic plates, which move very slowly against each other. Sometimes the edges get stuck, and the pressure builds up, until the rock suddenly slips and releases a great amount of energy, which travels outward as waves.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The point underground where the rock first slips is called the focus. The point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre, and that is usually where the shaking is strongest.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: There are two main kinds of wave. The P waves are the fastest, so they reach a recording station first. The S waves arrive later, and they do much more damage. The difference between their arrival times shows how far away the earthquake was.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The waves are recorded by an instrument called a seismograph, which draws a line that stays flat when the ground is still and wiggles when it shakes.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The best known measure is the Richter scale, devised in nineteen thirty-five by Charles Richter for the state of California. Each whole number on the scale means that the ground motion is ten times bigger, so a magnitude seven earthquake shakes the ground ten times as much as a magnitude six.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A different system, the Mercalli scale, measures the intensity of the shaking, not the energy released. It uses Roman numerals, and describes the effects, from hardly noticed to total destruction. So the same earthquake has one magnitude, but a different intensity in each place.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Many of the world's earthquakes occur around the Pacific Ocean, in a belt known as the Ring of Fire. Despite decades of research, earthquakes cannot be predicted, but early warning systems that detect the P waves can give people a few seconds of notice. Next week we'll look at tsunamis.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
